extracted.intended_audience: readers of Nature: scientists, naturalists, engineers, medical practitioners, and informed public
extracted.subtask_description: Short news items, book reviews, conference reports, prize notices and technical notes presenting evaluative criteria and procedural requirements for scientific work, publications, prizes, and technical apparatus as reported in a 1907 issue of Nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Denaturator requirements (alcohol denaturation prize)
rubrics_metrics.description: The denaturator must have a taste and smell which will effectually discourage any desire to use the alcohol as a beverage; wine or date must, oil of thyme and rosemary, and similar flavours are thus eliminated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Further constraints: It must not be so objectionable in smell as to prevent domestic or industrial use (thus acetylene, asafetida, and garlic are excluded); no soluble substance that could leave a deposit on lamp-wicks (e.g., sea-salt, sodium sulphate, alum, ammonium chloride, potassium ferrocyanide, picric acid, tobacco-juice, aloes) may be used; it must not consist of a substance much more or less volatile than alcohol (to avoid removal by fractional distillation) — ether, carbon bisulphide, light petroleum fractions, turpentine, cresyl, carbolic acid, camphor, naphthalene are excluded; it should contain no substance which might injure metallic parts of lamps or motors (ammonia, nitrobenzene, sulphuric acid); it should not be poisonous nor contain poison (e.g., mercuric chloride, methyl cyanide, sodium arseniate, aniline, hyoscyamus, aconite, digitalis); it should be sufficiently inexpensive; should not normally exist in commercial alcohol; and its presence in alcohol should be capable of easy and certain detection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alcohol-for-lighting system prize
rubrics_metrics.description: A second prize is offered for 'a system of utilising alcohol for lighting in the same manner as paraffin.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stated as the second prize accompanying the denaturator competition (value £2000); no further technical constraints given in this notice beyond the objective of using alcohol like paraffin for lighting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mangrove-bark extract for leather (German Colonial Society prize)
rubrics_metrics.description: Method to produce an extract from mangrove bark that will impart as much light and colour as possible to leather, and such as will only slightly darken by exposure to light.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Context/guidance: mangrove bark contains much tannin and a red colouring that prevents competition with other tanning agents; the practical problem is removal of this red colour; competitors invited to send particulars by a specified date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pressure-gauge performance criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: As regards freedom from friction and backlash, tested pressure gauges 'leave little to be desired'; but greater agreement between the records at different temperatures ought to be aimed at, and for gauges subject to vibration some form of balancing should be adopted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report based on tests at the National Physical Laboratory of ten first-class gauges; recommendation that improvements be driven by cooperation of manufacturers and institutions; emphasis on friction/backlash, temperature agreement, and balancing for vibration as key quality dimensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Validity of methods for measuring electric-spark (wireless) effective resistance
rubrics_metrics.description: Principal methods fall into two groups based on either the original resonance arrangement of Bjerknes or on the substitution process of Simons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dr. W. Eickhoff's examination concludes that the two groups give different results and that deductions as to the most suitable arrangements for telegraphic purposes cannot legitimately be made from results obtained by the method of Simons — i.e., not all measurement methods are equally valid for engineering inferences for wireless telegraphy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delegate submission requirements (Third International Sanitary Convention)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each delegate attending is expected to bring a paper relating to the nation represented by him, with a report on the existence of any transmissible diseases — especially bubonic plague, yellow fever, cholera, malaria, beri-beri, and trachoma — that may prevail within its boundaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Among the questions to be discussed are transmission of yellow fever, means to combat Stegomyia fasciata, tuberculosis, and various administrative measures; procedural expectation that delegates provide national reports on transmissible diseases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medical academy practical-year purpose and requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: After the university medical curriculum has been completed and the State examination passed, the practical year required by recent regulations may be spent at the academies (Düsseldorf, Cologne); the academies' object is to introduce newly qualified men to the practical side of medicine and to supply practitioners with opportunities for postgraduate study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structural arrangements (clinics and lecture-rooms) and clinical material should be abundant and excellent; the practical year and postgraduate work are emphasized as necessary complements to university training.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for genetic research evidence (critique of Mendelism reporting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mendel's proportions are treated as if they 'hold good for all subsequent progeny,' but Mendel never published figures proving long-term proportions, and many experiments were continued with small numbers; there is a need for repetition of experiments to test the Mendelian interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The notice urges a critical but constructive attitude: Mendelism produced discovery, but to validate interpretations investigators should deliberately repeat Mendel's experiments with sufficient sample sizes and publish figures across generations rather than rely on presumption; scientific proof requires replication and clear data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Game-coverts cultivation best practices (from 'Game and Game Coverts')
rubrics_metrics.description: Much greater care should be exercised by game-preservers as to the culture of covert suitable for different kinds of game: one kind of tree or bush is specially suited to particular species of game, and care is needed so that such trees or bushes may have proper opportunities for full development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and recommendations: blackberry bramble needs open space and sun to afford excellent covert and valuable food-supply; gamekeepers err in over-feeding their charges — it is often better to leave them to obtain their own living in properly planted coverts; attention to economic value of rabbits on estates; high-quality illustrative examples are valuable for landowners and game-preservers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trout-fishing instructional scope and audience expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: A volume titled 'How to Fish' is intended to instruct the beginner in the elementary principles of trout-fishing rather than to serve expert anglers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author treats methods beyond dry-fly fishing (spinning with minnows, luring with wasp-grub); the book should satisfy beginners, be well illustrated, and include observations on natural history and nature-study generally; contrasted with a more ambitious prior work intended for experts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lecture delivery & fee guidelines (Manchester Microscopical Society extension section)
rubrics_metrics.description: The work of lecturing and demonstrating is entirely voluntary and gratuitous on the part of the members, but a charge is made for the hire of slides, travelling, and out-of-pocket expenses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purpose is to bring scientific knowledge in a popular form before societies unable to pay large fees; additional fee is charged when lectures are given before commercial undertakings or societies subsidised out of government or public grants; all fees are devoted to the working expenses of the section.
